messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 47-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a park ranger in a large national forest in the Pacific Northwest. He presents for his first clinical intake with a PCL-5 score of 74, describing a presentation that has progressively worsened over the past several years following his experiences as a civilian caught in a prolonged armed conflict during a visit to relatives in West Africa in his late thirties. He has never previously sought mental health support, and describes himself as someone who "handled things alone" — a self-conception that has, over time, become both a coping strategy and a source of profound shame.

The events that brought Kwame to this point unfolded over several weeks in a region where fighting between armed factions had escalated suddenly. He had been staying in a rural village when militia forces moved through, burning homes and fields. He survived by hiding in dense bush while the fires spread around him, watching structures collapse and hearing sounds he has never been able to name aloud. Several people he had sheltered with did not survive. He made it out; they did not. He has carried that fact like a wound that never closed.

Kwame returned to the United States and resumed his work as a park ranger, a role that placed him — with devastating regularity — in the very landscape that most reliably pulls him back. The smell of controlled burns, the sight of smoke threading through tree canopy, or simply the quality of light falling across open grassland at dusk is enough to fracture his sense of where and when he is. In those moments, his body floods with alarm: his heart hammers, his breathing shortens, and the world around him narrows to something that feels imminently dangerous. He cannot relax even when he knows, intellectually, that he is safe — the knowledge sits in one part of his mind while his nervous system operates entirely independently of it. Sleep, when it comes at all, comes late and leaves early. He has learned to dread the hours between two and five in the morning, when there is nothing to occupy him and the memories move in freely.

What Kwame finds hardest to articulate — and what seems most central to his suffering — is the weight of his own self-judgment. He feels guilty for surviving. He is certain, in a way that resists logical challenge, that he acted in ways that violated who he understood himself to be during those weeks, though he is reluctant to specify what he means. He feels severed from other people, as though the experience placed him behind glass, able to observe ordinary life but unable to participate in it. These appraisals do not sit quietly — they actively return him to the trauma. When he feels the guilt rise, the images follow. When he feels the isolation sharpen, the sensory details of the burning village become more vivid, not less. The appraisals themselves function as internal triggers, keeping the wound open.

To manage this, Kwame has built a life of radical contraction. He avoids any contact with police or military uniforms — crossing the street, leaving shops, declining to attend his nephew's police academy graduation — because the sight of a uniform floods him with a dread he cannot contain. He has cut off nearly all contact with friends and family over the past three years, telling himself it is easier for everyone. He drinks most evenings, enough to dull the edge of hypervigilance and push sleep a little closer. But the isolation that was meant to protect him has deepened his sense of being set apart from humanity, feeding the very appraisals it was meant to quiet. The drinking blunts his alertness just enough to make the mornings worse, the threat-monitoring sharper, the assumption — when a radio call takes too long to come back or a trail goes unexpectedly quiet — that something terrible is already underway. And when his supervisor corrected his incident report last spring, a routine professional exchange, Kwame experienced it as an assault: his body responded as though danger had arrived, and he did not return to the ranger station for two days.

What finally brought him in was a controlled burn he was required to supervise last autumn. Standing at the perimeter of the flames, in uniform, in the forest, he lost several minutes entirely. He was found sitting on the ground by a colleague. He is most afraid, he says, that he will never be able to work outdoors again — and most afraid, beneath that, that he deserves exactly that.
